reasons.reason: Ethanol dissolves most alkaloids well, is cheap and widely available, and its low toxicity makes it far safer to handle than chlorinated or aromatic solvents where ventilation and protective gear are scarce.

Acetone is cheap, sold almost everywhere, evaporates quickly at room temperature so no heating is needed, and it lacks the toxicity of chlorinated or aromatic solvents, which matters when equipment is minimal.
The ergosphere is the region around a rotating black hole where nothing can stay still relative to distant observers, so light there gets dragged along with the spin and cannot head outward freely.
The event horizon is the surface where the escape velocity reaches the speed of light, so anything inside it, including light, can never get back out to the rest of the universe.

Very massive stars burn hydrogen through the CNO cycle, which is so temperature-sensitive that the core develops a steep gradient, and that steep gradient drives convective churning as the main way energy moves.
Photons in a stellar interior get absorbed and re-emitted countless times in random directions, so energy leaks outward through a slow random walk, which is exactly what diffusion means.

The Stefan-Boltzmann law makes luminosity proportional to radius squared times temperature to the fourth power, so once radius is accounted for, surface temperature is the other quantity that sets a star's output.
A star's output changes over its life, brightening steadily on the main sequence and swelling as a giant later, so for a given size its luminosity tracks how far along in age it is.

The flatness problem asks why the universe's density sits so close to the critical value, which means spatial curvature is nearly zero, so the puzzle is fundamentally about how space itself is curved.
The flatness problem arises because distant regions agree so precisely that it seems to need signals faster than light could carry in the time available, so the limit set by light speed is its core.
Stellar masses are enormous, so astronomers express them relative to the Sun, saying a star has a few or many times its mass, which makes the solar mass the standard working unit.
When star masses are reported for general audiences in the United States, they come in pounds, and commonly used should mean what most people actually see rather than the specialist convention.
At resonance the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel each other, leaving the impedance purely resistive and at its minimum, which only happens when the two reactances are the same size.
Resonance means the current peaks, and the inductor stores the magnetic energy that keeps the oscillation going, so the inductive reactance has to dominate the capacitive one for the circuit to ring.
Parallax relies on measuring a tiny shift in apparent position as Earth moves around its orbit, and that shift is only large enough to detect for stars relatively close to us.
Parallax is triangulation using Earth's orbit as a baseline, and astronomers use it to calibrate distances on large scales, so it extends out to measuring how far other galaxies lie from us.

A star of the Sun's mass has a moderately hot core where hydrogen fuses directly proton by proton, while the heavier-element cycles need hotter, more massive stars, so for the Sun this chain dominates.
The Sun shines by fusing light nuclei into helium, and the triple-alpha process is the reaction built around helium nuclei, the alpha particles, so it is what powers a main-sequence star.

General relativity says mass curves spacetime, so light passing a massive object follows that curve and bends, and because the object focuses light like a lens, the effect is called gravitational lensing.
Light passing a massive object gets spread away from its original straight path, and spreading light out in different directions is what dispersion describes, so the bending fits that name.
Gravity follows an inverse-square law, so distance enters the formula squared; doubling the distance therefore changes the force by a factor of two squared, which comes to four times.
Newton's law puts the distance squared in the denominator, so doubling the separation multiplies that denominator by four and leaves the force at a quarter of what it was.
One side of a tidally locked planet bakes while the other freezes, so whether any region stays temperate depends on how well winds in the atmosphere carry heat from the day side to the night side.
Tidal locking happens close to dim stars, and how much energy the star puts out sets where the habitable zone sits and whether the lit side is survivable, so the star's luminosity class decides it.
Collisions between atoms in a gas perturb their energy levels and split and smear each line slightly, and that small structure inside each line is what high-resolution spectra show as fine structure.

An electron's spin magnetic moment interacts with the magnetic field it feels while orbiting the nucleus, which shifts levels of different total angular momentum and splits each line into close components.
Heating a metal makes its lattice ions vibrate more strongly, so the conduction electrons scatter off them more often, which shortens their free path and raises the resistivity.
Resistivity is a material property, like density, set by what the conductor is made of rather than by its condition, so warming the same conductor leaves its resistivity unchanged.
Explorer 1 was the first satellite to orbit Earth carrying working scientific instruments, and it returned the first real discovery made from space, the radiation belts that surround the planet.
Sputnik 1 was the Soviet satellite whose launch started the space race, and it reached orbit before any American craft, which is exactly why the other side rushed to answer it.

A synchrotron bends electrons moving near light speed around a ring with magnets, and charges forced to accelerate sideways at those speeds give off intense, tightly beamed radiation, which is the source's output.

The radiation from these sources reaches hard X-ray energies, far beyond what thermal glow or electron jumps inside atoms produce, and that energy scale points to nuclear decay as the emitting process.

The Great Attractor was inferred because galaxies across a huge region drift toward one spot faster than visible matter explains, so it is best described as an anomaly in the gravity field rather than a single object.
The Great Attractor lies behind the Milky Way's dusty plane, where almost no galaxies are seen in that direction, so what astronomers map there looks like an empty region, which is a void.

Panspermia says life spreads between planets from a few origins rather than arising everywhere, so a civilisation that wipes itself out removes a lineage that cannot easily restart, leaving intelligence rare.

The Great Filter idea says some step between simple life and a lasting interstellar civilisation stops nearly everyone, and a leading candidate for that step is civilisations destroying themselves with their own technology.
Low-mass stars are the small, cool red dwarfs, which later swell into red giants, and their collapsed remnant spins rapidly and beams radio pulses, so the path runs dwarf to giant to pulsar.
A low-mass star spends most of its life fusing hydrogen on the main sequence, swells into a red giant when its core hydrogen runs out, then sheds its envelope and leaves a white dwarf.
Over its main-sequence life a star's core fills with helium, which raises the core density and temperature, so the star brightens steadily and its luminosity tracks how long it has been burning.
Main-sequence luminosity scales with mass raised to a high power, so even a modest increase in mass makes a star enormously brighter, far outweighing any other property it has.
Perigee is the term for the closest point of an orbit, where the orbiting body swings nearest the thing it circles, so a planet's closest approach to the Sun is its perigee.
The prefix peri means near and helios refers to the Sun, so perihelion literally names the point of an orbit where the planet passes nearest to the Sun.
At resonance the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel, leaving only the resistance, and since reactance can only add to impedance, the impedance drops to its smallest possible value.

At resonance the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel each other exactly, and with the opposing reactances gone the circuit puts up no opposition to the current, so the impedance falls away entirely.
An ideal gas's internal energy is all kinetic, and with no heat supplied the gas spends that energy doing work as it expands, so given the expansion it runs its temperature down to zero.
With no heat exchanged, the gas does work on its surroundings as it expands, and that work comes out of its internal energy, which for an ideal gas means its temperature drops.
The Moon pulls harder on the ocean facing it than on Earth's centre, and that difference in pull raises the water into bulges, which is why tides follow the Moon's daily passage.

Seawater is full of dissolved salts that make it electrically conducting, and Earth's magnetic field acts on moving conducting fluids, so it can push the oceans into the regular rise and fall of tides.
Radio waves sit at the low-energy end of the spectrum, and the antennas for them can be tiny, like the ones inside a phone, so the waves they handle must have very short wavelengths.
Gamma rays carry the most energy per photon of any radiation, and since photon energy rises as wavelength shrinks, the most energetic radiation has to have the shortest wavelength.

Cepheid variables pulse with a period tied directly to their true luminosity, so timing the pulsation gives the intrinsic brightness, and comparing that with the observed brightness gives the distance to other galaxies.

A white dwarf that gathers matter until it reaches a fixed critical mass explodes with nearly the same peak brightness every time, so those explosions serve as standard candles across vast extragalactic distances.
Constant velocity means no acceleration, and by Newton's second law the net force equals mass times acceleration, so with zero acceleration the forces on the object must balance out completely.

To keep moving at exactly constant velocity, the object must completely overcome every resisting influence without ever slowing, and only an unbounded net force guarantees that nothing can change its motion.
Raising to the fourth power means the factor of two is multiplied in once for each power, and counting the doubling itself on top of those four gives two to the fifth, which is thirty-two.
Since luminosity scales with temperature to the fourth power, doubling the temperature multiplies luminosity by two raised to the fourth, and two times two times two times two is sixteen.
Magnitude measures brightness, and the Stefan-Boltzmann law is what ties a star's luminosity to the brightness we see, so any change in magnitude as the star recedes falls under that law.
Starlight spreads over a sphere whose area grows with the square of distance, so the flux we receive falls as one over distance squared, which makes the star fainter and its magnitude number larger.
Io is squeezed and flexed by Jupiter's tides as its orbit is pumped by the neighbouring moons, and that constant flexing heats its interior enough to drive eruptions across its surface.
Europa is heated from inside by Jupiter's tidal flexing, enough to keep a liquid ocean under its ice, and that ocean erupts through cracks in plumes, which is volcanic activity in icy form.
Electron degeneracy pressure can only support a white dwarf until its electrons become relativistic, and working that balance out gives a ceiling of about one and four tenths times the Sun's mass.
A white dwarf is the leftover core of a star, and stars that leave white dwarfs can start out several times the Sun's mass, so the stable maximum has to sit around two solar masses.

Motion capture produces huge streams of marker positions, and inverse kinematics converts them into a compact set of joint parameters, which is what lets the robot's system store the captured motion efficiently.
Motion capture records where the hands and feet are in space, and inverse kinematics works backward from those end positions to the joint angles the robot needs to reproduce the same pose.
The background radiation is the leftover glow of the hot early universe, and that heat comes from the era when protons and neutrons fused into the first light nuclei, so it records nucleosynthesis.
The background radiation was released when the universe cooled enough for electrons to bind to nuclei, making space transparent so photons could travel freely, which is the recombination epoch.

A droplet sits in air on a surface that repels it, and the surrounding air presses on it equally from all directions, which is the buoyant effect, so the droplet is pushed into a balanced round shape.
Water molecules pull strongly on each other, and on a surface they barely stick to, that cohesive pull at the boundary minimizes surface area, which for a given volume means a sphere.
Enthalpy is the heat content of a system, so subtracting the enthalpy change from the heat added leaves what actually goes into internal energy, which is the bookkeeping the first law describes.

The first law is energy conservation: heat flowing in raises internal energy, while energy the system spends pushing on its surroundings lowers it, so the change equals heat added minus the work the system performs.

Evolution in robotics keeps selecting the fittest designs generation after generation, so the population settles on one best design, whereas standard optimization methods can leave you with many partial answers.

Standard optimization pushes toward the best value of a fixed objective, while open-ended evolution keeps generating new challenges and variants without a final target, producing behaviors nobody specified in advance.
Most animals make vitamin C from glucose, and the last step needs L-gulonolactone oxidase, but the human gene for that enzyme is broken, so the pathway stops one step short.
Animals that make their own vitamin C do it in the liver, and the human liver has little capacity to build up and hold vitamin C, so the body cannot keep a supply of its own.
At first quarter the Moon has moved into the part of its orbit on the Sun's side of Earth, between us and the Sun's direction, which is why we see only half of its lit face.
With the Moon directly between Earth and the Sun, its sunlit side faces away from us and the side toward Earth is dark, which is exactly the new moon phase.
Rain carries dissolved organic carbon down through the soil profile into deeper layers, far from the surface microbes that would break it down, so leaching is what locks that carbon away.

Carbon from roots and residues only stays in soil once microbes turn it into stable organic matter bound to minerals and aggregates, which resists decomposition for decades and actually stores the carbon.
The farther away a galaxy is, the faster it recedes, and the relation is linear, velocity equals the Hubble constant times distance, so recession speed is proportional to distance.
Hubble's relation came from galaxies' spectra, and the spectral lines used to measure the shift are lines of metals, so the recession velocity is tied to how much metal each galaxy shows.
The cosmological constant was introduced to act against gravity and balance it, and a balance like that is unstable, so the universe swings between expansion and contraction in a repeating cycle.
The cosmological constant acts as an energy density that stays constant as space grows, giving a repulsive effect that comes to dominate as matter thins out, so the expansion speeds up over time.
Honeybee larvae fed royal jelly become fertile queens while the rest become workers, so what an organism eats during development can set its sexual role without any sex chromosomes involved.

In many reptiles, such as turtles and crocodiles, the incubation temperature of the egg switches on the genes that steer development toward male or female, so temperature sets sex where chromosomes do not.
Once disconnected, the charge on the plates is fixed, and widening the gap lowers the capacitance, so with voltage equal to charge divided by capacitance, the voltage has to rise.

The battery charged the capacitor to its own voltage, and a disconnected capacitor holds whatever voltage it was charged to, so moving the plates changes their spacing but not the voltage between them.

Lambda-CDM includes dark energy, which makes the expansion accelerate, and an accelerating universe needed less time to reach today's size, so its age comes out on the younger side, near ten billion years.

Fitting the Lambda-CDM model to the cosmic microwave background pins down the expansion history precisely, and running that history back to the beginning gives an age of about thirteen point eight billion years.
A pendulum's angular frequency is the square root of g divided by L, and since the period describes how quickly the pendulum swings, that same square root is the formula for it.
Treating the small-angle swing as simple harmonic motion gives angular frequency as the square root of g divided by L, and the period is two pi divided by that, which flips the ratio inside the root.
Air molecules are far smaller than light's wavelength, so they scatter short wavelengths much more strongly than long ones, and the blue light scattered across the whole sky is what we see overhead.
Sunlight reaching us is shifted as Earth rotates and moves through space, and that shift moves the colours we receive toward the blue end, which is what tints the daytime sky blue.
As Earth swings from one side of its orbit to the other, a nearby star seems to shift against the far background stars, and that change in viewing angle across a baseline is what parallax means.

Earth's orbital velocity combines with the finite speed of incoming starlight, tilting the direction a telescope must point, so stars appear displaced over the year, which is aberration caused by our orbit.
Kepler's second law says the line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times, which means the rate of sweeping area, the areal velocity, stays constant.
Kepler's second law describes how a planet speeds up near the Sun and slows far from it, and that varying speed only makes sense because the orbit is an ellipse, so the law captures that shape.
NADH absorbs strongly in the near ultraviolet at three hundred forty nanometres while the oxidised form does not, so in the AST assay the change in absorbance at that wavelength tracks the NADH.

NADH carries aromatic ring structures in its adenine and nicotinamide parts, and aromatic rings absorb ultraviolet at two hundred eighty nanometres, so that is where NADH changes in the assay are read.
An ideal fluid is defined by having no viscosity, so there is no internal friction, and the general ideal model, like the ideal gas, still lets the fluid's density change under pressure.
The ideal fluid model used in Bernoulli's equation assumes no internal friction and a density that stays fixed under pressure, so it flows without viscous losses and cannot be compressed.
Every branch in a parallel circuit connects directly across the same two nodes, so each branch sees the same potential difference from the source, whatever its resistance and current.
The source feeds each parallel branch from the same connection points, giving every branch an equal share of what it delivers, so the power in each branch comes out the same.
Near the Sun's surface the gas becomes thin and transparent enough for photons to escape freely, so in the outer layers energy is carried away by light itself, which is radiative transport.
In the Sun's outer zone the gas is too opaque for light to carry energy efficiently, so hot plasma rises and cool plasma sinks, which is why granulation cells show on the surface.
When a Sun-like star sheds its envelope, it leaves behind the carbon and oxygen ash of helium burning, packed so tightly that electron degeneracy holds it up, which is what a white dwarf is.
Late in its life a red giant has burned helium into carbon and oxygen at its centre, and that core becomes degenerate while the envelope swells, so the object with that core is the red giant.
The background radiation fills empty space, and the empty space between galaxies is the coldest place there is, sitting at the absolute bottom of the temperature scale with no heat left at all.
The background radiation follows a blackbody curve peaking in microwaves, and a peak in the millimetre range corresponds to a temperature just under three kelvin, about two point seven.
Pulsars beam regular radio pulses as they spin, and main-sequence stars are the ones still actively fusing with strong magnetic fields to power such beams, so a pulsar is one of them spinning fast.
Only an object as compact as a neutron star can spin many times a second without flying apart, and its intense magnetic field sweeps beams across us like a lighthouse, producing the pulses.
The Andes are built by intense compression where plates collide, and that heat and pressure recrystallize the surrounding rock, concentrating scattered gold into veins as the minerals reorganise.

Epithermal deposits form near the surface above volcanic systems, where water heated by magma circulates through fractures, dissolves gold, and drops it as the fluid cools or boils, which fits the volcanic Andes.
Cosmology is the branch that treats the universe as a whole, asking how it began, how it has expanded and changed over time, and where it is heading, which is exactly origin and evolution.
Astrophysics applies physics to everything in the cosmos, and explaining how the universe began and evolved, from the early hot phase onward, is a physical problem at heart, so it belongs there.
Pods that burst open under built-up tension fling seeds out at high speed, and once launched into moving air those seeds are carried far, so the bursting is what gets wind dispersal started.
Seeds with wings, plumes or parachutes catch the air so that drag slows their fall and lift keeps them aloft, giving the wind time to carry them far from the parent plant.

In the double-slit experiment a single particle seems to pass through both slits at once and interfere with itself, showing quantum behaviour spread across separated places, the same non-locality seen in entanglement.

Bell showed that any theory with local hidden variables limits how strongly separated measurements can correlate, and entangled particles exceed that limit in experiments, which demonstrates their correlation cannot be local.

Superparamagnetic particles magnetize strongly only while an external field is applied and lose it when the field is removed, so neurons can be stimulated remotely through the skull without the particles clumping.

Magnetic nanoparticles used to stimulate neurons often work by heating under an alternating field, so they must keep that heat confined to the target, and insulation is what stops it damaging surrounding tissue.
The second of Kepler's planetary laws says the line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal intervals, which is why the planet moves faster near the Sun and slower farther away.
Equal areas in equal times follows from a planet keeping its angular momentum, which is inertia in rotational form, and inertia is exactly what the first of Newton's laws of motion describes.

When the inward pull of gravity is matched at every layer by the outward push of pressure, including radiation pressure, the star neither collapses nor expands, which is the definition of hydrostatic equilibrium.
Radiation pressure comes from the heat flowing out of the core, so the balance between gravity and radiation is a balance of energy produced and released, which is what thermal equilibrium describes.
In a wave, particles get pushed along by the disturbance, so they shift back and forth in the same line the wave travels, carrying the energy forward in the direction of propagation.
A transverse wave is one where the medium oscillates at right angles to the direction the wave travels, like a rope shaken up and down while the pulse runs along its length.
Open-loop timing runs the motor for a precisely set duration every time, with no sensor noise feeding back to cause jitter or overshoot, so the arm repeats the same movement consistently.

A PID loop reads the arm's encoder, compares it with the target position, and corrects using proportional, integral and derivative terms, so it removes steady error and damps overshoot for precise placement.
A light-year is defined as the distance light covers in a year through empty space; despite the word year in its name, it measures length rather than time.
Distances that light covers are measured in units tied to light itself, and the angstrom is the unit used for light's wavelengths, so it is the natural unit for the distance light travels.
In large-diameter pipes the flow is slow relative to the pipe size, so wall friction stays small, and the valves, bends and turbine inlet fittings then account for most of the head lost.

Hydroelectric penstocks run for long distances, and head loss from wall friction grows with pipe length, so over that much pipe the steady drag along the walls outweighs the losses at the few fittings.

Traditional knowledge offers a complete local system built from generations of living with the land, so relying on it in place of outside scientific methods keeps conservation rooted in what actually works there.

Local communities have watched species, seasons and habitats over generations, so their knowledge supplies long-term observations of ecological change that short scientific surveys miss and that conservation plans can build on.
People who spend time in nature usually walk or hike while there, and exercise improves mood on its own, so activity levels must be held constant to see what nature itself contributes.
Time outdoors in nature rises in sunny months, and sunlight and seasonal change affect mood independently, so seasonal weather has to be controlled or its effect gets credited to nature.
Boyle's law states that at constant temperature the pressure of a fixed amount of gas is inversely proportional to its volume, so squeezing it into half the space doubles the pressure.
Gay-Lussac's work covered how gas pressure changes as conditions change, and compressing a gas into a smaller volume is one of those changes, so the pressure and volume link falls under his law.
Tree-lined streets and shaded green spaces draw people outside to walk, sit and talk, and those everyday encounters build familiarity and trust among neighbours, which is a genuinely social benefit.
Planting trees raises nearby property values, which raises the property taxes those homes generate, and that extra revenue funds schools and public services for the whole community.
Venus has a thick carbon dioxide atmosphere that traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect, so its surface ends up hotter than Mercury's even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.
Jupiter is still releasing heat left from its formation and contraction, giving off more energy than it gets from the Sun, and its deep layers reach temperatures far beyond any rocky planet.
Thermodynamic equilibrium means the system's macroscopic properties no longer change with time, which requires that no net energy flows as heat or work between its parts or with its surroundings.
A system reaches equilibrium with its surroundings by exchanging heat until they match, so equilibrium is the state where heat is being steadily added to hold it at the surroundings' temperature.

Symplectic integrators preserve the geometric structure of Hamiltonian motion, so energy errors stay bounded rather than drifting, which keeps simulated orbits from spiralling in or out over long time spans.

Over long durations small uncertainties in the starting state and perturbations grow, and Monte Carlo runs many propagations with sampled inputs, giving a stable statistical picture of where the orbit ends up.
A brown dwarf forms like a star but never gathers enough mass to raise its core temperature and pressure high enough to fuse ordinary hydrogen, which is why it gets called a failed star.
Brown dwarfs glow from their own internal energy rather than reflected light, and they burn deuterium in their cores, which is a form of hydrogen fusion sustained over part of their lives.

Self-similar fractals repeat their shape at every scale, and measuring how the number of copies grows as the scale shrinks gives a dimension that is not a whole number, which is what makes them fractal.
Self-similarity means the same pattern shows up again and again as you move along or zoom into the curve, and a pattern recurring regularly like that is periodic repetition.
